origin_region: Central and Rift Valley highlands · Nandi Hills, Kericho, Nyeri, Kirinyaga, Meru
cultivar: Kenyan clones (TRFK series) of Assam-type stock, with some Chinary plantings for speciality lots
processing: Fully oxidised orthodox manufacture: a longer wither than CTC, whole-leaf rolling, full oxidation and firing, then sorting into leaf grades; a small but growing share of Kenyan output, some of it hand-rolled at speciality factories.
harvest_season: Year-round; dry-season lots (January–February, July–September) are brighter and more aromatic.
appearance_dry: Long, well-twisted black leaf, often with golden tips.
taste_profile: Fuller and sweeter than the CTC: malt, dark honey and dried fruit with a brisk, citrusy lift and a clean finish.

brewing.notes: Just under the boil, 3–4 minutes; try it without milk first, and expect a second steep.

vintage_note: Sold mainly by direct trade and speciality importers as named-factory lots, sometimes with a plucking month (Kangaita, a KTDA factory in Kirinyaga, Emrok in Nandi and several cooperative factories are names that come up); a few orthodox grades also pass through the Mombasa auction. Buy the current year's lot and use within about 18 months.
description:
Kenyan orthodox is the small but growing share of Kenya's tea that is rolled whole rather than cut into CTC granules: long, twisted black leaf from the same equatorial highlands around Nandi, Kericho, Nyeri and Meru that supply the world's tea bags. It exists because a few factories and smallholder groups realised that the bright, theaflavin-rich Kenyan leaf, given a longer wither and gentler handling, makes a speciality tea that can stand next to an Assam or a Ceylon.

Manufacture is conventional orthodox: a longer wither than CTC, whole-leaf rolling, full oxidation and firing, then sorting into leaf grades; some of the speciality factories hand-roll small lots, and the same places often make white, green and purple teas on the side. The leaf is plucked year-round, and the dry-season lots are brighter and more aromatic.

The cup is bright copper-amber, fuller and sweeter than the CTC: malt, dark honey and dried fruit with a brisk, citrusy lift and a clean finish. Brew it with water just under the boil for three to four minutes, try it without milk first, and expect a second steep.

It is sold mainly by direct trade and speciality importers as named-factory lots, sometimes with a plucking month; Kangaita (a KTDA factory in Kirinyaga), Emrok in Nandi and several cooperative factories are names that come up, and a few orthodox grades also pass through the Mombasa auction. Buy the current year's lot and use it within eighteen months.

A good tea for anyone who dismissed Kenya as 'tea-bag country'; the leaf was always this good, it was just cut up.
